content: Dysuria occurs as a result of the contraction of the bladder muscles and the peristaltic movements of the urethra. These processes cause urine to come into contact with the inflamed mucosal lining of the urinary tract. This contact stimulates pain receptors, leading to sensations of pain or burning during urination. Epidemiology Dysuria can affect both males and females. However, one of the most common causes of dysuria is a urinary tract infection (UTI). UTIs are significantly more prevalent in females than in males due to anatomical differences. Females have a shorter and straighter urethra compared to males, whose urethra is longer and curved. In females, the shorter and straighter urethra allows bacteria to reach the bladder more easily, as the distance they need to travel is reduced. Additionally, females who use improper wiping techniques, such as wiping from back to front instead of front to back, are at a higher risk of developing UTIs. This is because the urethral opening is anatomically closer to the rectum, increasing the likelihood of bacterial contamination. Consequently, females are more likely to experience dysuria compared to males. Pathophysiology Dysuria caused by inflammatory conditions, such as a urinary tract infection, arises from the contraction of the bladder muscles and urethral peristalsis. These actions bring urine into contact with the inflamed mucosal lining, which stimulates sensory nerves and pain receptors. This stimulation results in pain, often accompanied by sensations of burning, stinging, or itching during urination. The sensitivity of these pain receptors can be heightened during inflammatory or neuropathic processes. In some cases, inflammation from surrounding organs, such as the colon, can also contribute to the development of dysuria. If dysuria is caused by renal stones, treatment options depend on the size and location of the stones. Stones smaller than 5 mm typically pass spontaneously. Patients are advised to maintain adequate hydration and strain their urine to confirm the passage of the stone. For stones larger than 5 mm, various treatment modalities are available, including extracorporeal shock wave lithotripsy (ESWL), percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL), or open surgical intervention. In males, when dysuria is associated with chronic prostatitis, oral antibiotics may be considered as a treatment option. However, this should only be initiated after obtaining a urine culture to guide appropriate antibiotic therapy.
